summary:
New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, compiled by applying a rubric to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking places the state among jurisdictions whose laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

State law effective 1 July 2003 prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership. The 1 July 2019 repeal of the fifteen-employee exemption extended employment coverage to smaller employers, and 2023 legislation passed under an emergency clause explicitly extended protection to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies. Albuquerque amended its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align with that expansion.

New Mexico's hate-crime statute has explicitly covered violence committed because of actual or perceived gender identity since 2003. School-bullying legislation passed in March 2019, effective 1 July 2019, protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies.

Since 1 November 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery, under legislation that repealed the 1984 surgery requirement and provides male, female and X neutral designation on birth certificates, driver's licences and state IDs. The bill passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and was signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. An applicant submits a Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with the applicable fees, with parental consent for minors, and a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licences and IDs. This replaced the prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician attesting surgical change, together with a certified name-change order.

Since 1 July 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral and available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex; the legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and was signed by the Governor.

In March 2023 HB7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sexual reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions, including for travellers from other jurisdictions, making New Mexico a sanctuary state for transgender youth. The same session's HB31 repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper, which had endangered the privacy and safety of transgender individuals. In 2026 the state health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule moved to exclude it.

The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists New Mexico as a state holding a shield law or 2023 executive order. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is legal in New Mexico has been banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a state with a care ban.

Omnibus crime bill HB68, passed in February 2022 and signed 9 March 2022, repealed the common-law gay and trans panic defence. No state law prohibits transgender girls from school sports participation; eligibility is determined by the original or amended birth certificate, and the New Mexico Activities Association has issued no further guidance.

Same-sex couples have held the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the state Supreme Court ruling of 19 December 2013, and statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019, signed in April and effective 1 July 2019. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex is covered by state recognition.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 ranking's contrast tier shows how far the state sits from the worst-law jurisdictions: those carry up to five-year prison terms for gender identity in one state and an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use in another.

The same MAP page records the national shield landscape as of 27 September 2026: 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none. Youth-care bans are tracked on the page, some permanently blocked.

Statewide polling showed 73% support in 2018 for anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people, and 64% support in 2017 for a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

Several Indigenous nations of the region historically recognised four gender roles, including the Navajo nadleehi, a male-bodied person with a feminine nature who, because of a perceived balance between the sexes, was typically chosen for communal and spiritual roles, wore female clothing, did female work and could have sexual relations with men, which the tribe accepted. Comparable recognised roles existed among the Zuni (lhamana and katsotse) and among Mescalero Apache, Tiwa, Tewa and other pueblos. Colonisation eroded much of this acceptance: nadleehi became a subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among the Hopi were barred from the traditional snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. A writer on Indigenous gender diversity documented that accounts of the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" were used by Spanish explorers to argue for colonisation of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity.
localsOnly:
State law effective 1 July 2003 also prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, supplemented by a 1985 executive order barring sexual-orientation discrimination in public employment. Enforcement of that provision was upheld unanimously in Elane Photography v. Willock in 2013, over a refusal to photograph a same-sex commitment ceremony. The hate-crime statute has covered actual or perceived sexual orientation since 2003, and the March 2019 bullying legislation covers sexual orientation from 1 July 2019.

Sexual orientation change efforts on minors are prohibited under SB121, passed 32-6 in the Senate and 44-23 in the House, signed 7 April 2017 by Governor Susana Martinez and effective 6 July 2017.

Single persons, same-sex couples and second-parent adoptions are permitted with no prohibition. Lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization and donor insemination regardless of sexual orientation or marital status, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised as a legal parent, and no statute or case law prohibits gestational or traditional surrogacy, which courts generally recognise.

State-employee benefits have been extended to same-sex partners since 2003, with statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019, signed in April by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham and effective 1 July 2019. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since repeal of the anti-sodomy law in 1975, and a 1986 attempt to reinstate it failed.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory documents no incidents of anti-trans violence, arrests or enforcement actions inside New Mexico. Whether the state hate-crime statute or the 2019 bullying requirements have been applied in any specific case here is unresolved in these sources.

The figure that 70% of LGBT Navajo youth have attempted suicide is undated and covers LGBT youth as a whole rather than trans people specifically, so it cannot be read as a current trans-specific risk measure.

How the state shield law would operate against a federal enforcement action, and whether any test of it has occurred, is not sourced.

The rubric and its weighting behind the July 2026 tier placement are not published in the source, so the ranking cannot be independently verified from this inventory.

Beyond birth-certificate eligibility, the New Mexico Activities Association has issued no guidance, and how an eligibility dispute would be resolved is not documented.
